Kleisli convolution representations of power monoids

The authors are normally listed alphabetically by surname. In this submission, however, Haicun Wen is placed as the first author to satisfy the doctoral graduation requirement of Northwest Normal University.
Haicun Wen    Jian He    Yu-Zhe Liu
  1. 1

    College of Mathematics and Statistics, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, China;

    E-mail: Wenhaicun1990@163.com (H. Wen)

  2. 2

    Department of Applied Mathematics, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China;

    E-mail: jianhe30@163.com (J. He)

  3. 3

    School of Mathematics and Statistics, Guizhou University, Guiyang 550025, Guizhou, China;

    E-mail: liuyz@gzu.edu.cn / yzliu3@163.com (Y.-Z Liu)

  1. ORCID: 0009-0007-6552-1703

  2. ORCID: 0009-0007-6001-1851

  3. ORCID: 0009-0005-1110-386X

Abstract: We show that power semigroups of groups, and more generally reduced finitary power monoids, arise naturally as convolution monoids in Kleisli categories of powerset monads:

  • •

    for the non-empty powerset monad, the Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) is isomorphic to the power monoid 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G);

  • •

    for the reduced finite powerset monad on pointed sets, the Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})} (ℤ/2​ℤ,H)(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) is isomorphic to the reduced finitary power monoid 𝒫fin,1​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H).

This unifies several constructions in power semigroup theory: Kleisli convolution representations of semigroups, base change along surjective group homomorphisms, and rigidity of automorphism groups. As an application, we prove that for every proper numerical monoid SS, the Kleisli Hom-monoid Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S) is rigid. This gives a proof of the Tringali–Yan conjecture in the language of Kleisli categories. It should be mentioned that this conjecture was already proved by Bhowmik and Tringali in a preprint posted on arXiv on July 25, 2026.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 18C15 18D15 20M30 20M50

Keywords: Kleisli category; Kleisli arrow; Kleisli point

1 Introduction

Let HH be a semigroup. The multiplication of HH extends to its non-empty subsets by AB:={ab:a∈A,b∈B}AB:=\{ab:a\in A,\ b\in B\}. The resulting power semigroup is a classical construction in semigroup theory, going back at least to the works of Tamura and Shafer in [20]. One of its basic structural questions asks to what extent the power semigroup determines the original semigroup. This question led to the study of globally determined classes and related isomorphism problems, see for example [14, 11, 10, 18, 16, 17]. Standard background on semigroups and their representations may be found in [12]. For a monoid HH, 𝒫fin,1​(H)={A⊆H:A​ is finite and ​1H∈A}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H)=\{A\subseteq H:A\text{ is finite and }1_{H}\in A\} is also a monoid, and we call it the reduced finitary power monoid of HH. Power monoids have recently been studied from the viewpoints of factorization theory and arithmetic combinatorics [9, 5, 6, 7, 19]. For numerical monoids, the ambient additive order supplies particularly effective tools, where the required background on numerical monoids is given in [2]. Automorphism groups and rigidity phenomena for finitary or reduced power monoids have been determined in several important cases, including ℕ\mathbb{N}, ℤ\mathbb{Z}, finite abelian groups, and numerical monoids [15, 21, 24, 22, 26]. Related results concerning torsion groups and the Bienvenu–Geroldinger conjecture appear in [23, 25].

The Kleisli construction is one of the standard categorical constructions associated with a monad, and it is the origin of Kleisli categories, which were initially introduced for the study of adjoint functors, see [13, 8, etc]. The main purpose of this paper is to show that power semigroups of groups, and more generally reduced finitary power monoids, are naturally instances of convolution in Kleisli categories. To be precise, for the set category 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}, one can define two special triples 𝒫+=(𝒫+,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{+}=(\mathcal{P}_{+},\eta,\mu) and 𝒫fin=(𝒫fin,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}=(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}},\eta,\mu) and obtain two Kleisli categories 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+}) and 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}), respectively. Then the two Kleisli categories have natural monoidal category structures (𝐒𝐞𝐭,⊗,{∗})(\mathbf{Set},\otimes,\{*\}), and, for any two Kleisli morphisms f,g:X↝Yf,g:X\rightsquigarrow Y (say also Kleisli arrows) in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(X,Y)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(X,Y) (the case for f,g∈Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(X,Y)f,g\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(X,Y) is similar), we have a convolution

Here, Δ\Delta is a comultiplication defined on XX, and mm is a multiplication defines on 𝒫+​(Y):={A⊆Y:A≠∅}\mathcal{P}_{+}(Y):=\{A\subseteq Y:A\neq\varnothing\}. Based on the above, we obtain the first main result of this paper.

Theorem A (Theorem 2.16, Lemma 3.4).

For any group GG, 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) and the Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) are monoids ((the multiplication in this Kleisli Hom-space is the convolution “⋆\star” as above)), and we have an isomorphism

Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)≅𝒫+​(G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G)\cong\mathcal{P}_{+}(G)

of monoids. The same assertion holds with 𝒫+\mathscr{P}_{+} replaced by 𝒫fin\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}.

Here, the object 11 in the Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+}) (or 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})) is a one-point set in 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}. The categorical perspective given in Theorem A makes the multiplication of subsets appear not as an ad hoc extension of the original multiplication, but as the canonical convolution arising from the monoidal structure of the Kleisli category. Now, we have a natural question that what is 𝒫+​(q)\mathcal{P}_{+}(q) (or 𝒫fin​(q)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(q)) for homomorphism q:F→Gq:F\to G of groups FF and GG? The following theorem provides an answer for this question, and shows that: each Kleisli arrow in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) can be lifted to a Kleisli arrow in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,F)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,F); and this lift is convolution-preserving.

Theorem B (Theorem 3.7).

Every surjective homomorphism q:F→Gq:F\to G of groups induces an embedding

q†:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)↪Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,F)q^{{\dagger}}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,F)

sends each Kleisli point fA:1={∗}↝Gf_{A}:1=\{*\}\rightsquigarrow G ((defined by 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁fA​(∗)=A⊆G)f_{A}(*)=A\subseteq G) in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) to the Kleisli point fq−1​(A):1↝Ff_{q^{-1}(A)}:1\rightsquigarrow F ((satisfying 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁fq−1​(A)​(∗)=q−1​(A)⊆F)f_{q^{-1}(A)}(*)={q^{-1}(A)}\subseteq F) in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,F)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,F).

Let 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} be the pointed set category, which can be seen as a subcategory of 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} (up to some embedding), whose object is a pairs (X,∗)(X,*), say pointed set, of a set XX and an element ∗∈X*\in X, and whose morphism (X,∗)→(Y,∘)(X,*)\to(Y,\circ) is a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y with f(∗)=∘f(*)=\circ. Then we can define 𝒫fin,∗(X,∗):=({A⊆X:A is finite and ∗∈A},{∗})\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*):=\bigl(\{A\subseteq X:A\text{ is finite and }*\in A\},\{*\}\bigr) for each pointed set (X,∗)(X,*). We can naturally induce a triple 𝒫fin=(𝒫fin,−,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}=(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-},\eta,\mu) over 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} by using the monad 𝒫+,fin\mathscr{P}_{+,\mathrm{fin}} given in the previous text. In this paper, we show the following important fact.

Theorem C (Theorem 4.1).

The triple 𝒫fin=(𝒫fin,−,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}=(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-},\eta,\mu) is a monad over 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}.

This theorem shows that we can build a Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}) over 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}. Another purpose of this paper is to discuss numerical monoids and their reduced finitary power monoids under this Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}), and we can study the rigidity of the automorphism group of power monoids. Here, for a monoid H=(H,⋅)H=(H,\cdot), its reduced finitary power monoid is defined as 𝒫fin,1​(H):={A⊆H:A​ is finite and ​1∈A}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H):=\{A\subseteq H:A\text{ is finite and }1\in A\}. The following theorem provides a description of the reduced finitary power monoid of a monoid HH.

Theorem D (Theorem 4.4).

For every monoid HH, pointed by its identity element 1H1_{H}, there is a natural bijection

θfin,H:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin,∗)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)→𝒫fin,1H​(H)\theta_{\mathrm{fin},H}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H)\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H)

of monoids.

Parallel to Theorem B, we have the following theorem.

Let q:F↠ℤq:F\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z} be a surjective group homomorphism. Then, for any numerical monoid SS, the following statements hold.

Finally, we consider an application to the Tringali–Yan conjecture. Tringali and Yan conjectured that 𝒫fin,0​(S)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) is rigid whenever SS is a numerical monoid properly contained in ℕ\mathbb{N}, see [24, Section 4]. This conjecture was proved by Bhowmik and Tringali in [4, Theorem 1.2]. Their proof is shorter than the Kleisli proof given in this paper. By using the isomorphism

Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)≅𝒫fin,0​(S),\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)\cong\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S),

we restate the relevant arguments in terms of Kleisli arrows and Kleisli convolution. In particular, we prove that

Aut⁡(Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S))≅{1}\operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S))\cong\{1\}

for every numerical monoid SS properly contained in ℕ\mathbb{N}, see Theorem 5.9. The purpose of this application is to show that Kleisli convolution representations may provide a useful categorical viewpoint for problems in semigroup theory.

2 Powerset monads and convolution

Throughout the paper, a semigroup need not have an identity, whereas a monoid does. For a set XX, let 𝒫+​(X):={A⊆X:A≠∅}\mathcal{P}_{+}(X):=\{A\subseteq X:A\neq\varnothing\} and let 𝒫fin​(X):={A⊆X:0<|A|<∞}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X):=\{A\subseteq X:0<|A|<\infty\}. The symbols 𝒫+\mathcal{P}_{+} and 𝒫fin\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}} will retain these meanings throughout. In particular, 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) never includes the empty set.

We have verified only (M1), because (M2)–(M4) are not axioms requiring proof. Clause (M2) merely introduces the terminology “Kleisli arrows” for morphisms X→T​YX\to TY; clause (M3) defines the Kleisli composition rule using the already-established μ\mu; and clause (M4) defines the identity morphism using the already-established η\eta. These are constructions that become available once the monad structure from (M1) has been proven. They are not additional conditions that 𝒫+\mathscr{P}_{+} must satisfy. ∎

Remark 2.4.

Recall that a monad (T,η,μ)(T,\eta,\mu) is called a strong monad if it together with a natural transformation

stX,Y:X×T​Y⟶T⁡(X×Y),\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}:X\times TY\longrightarrow T(X\times Y),

called the strength, satisfying the following strength axioms:

  1. (SM1)

    stX,Y∘(idX×ηY)=ηX×Y\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{X}\times\eta_{Y})=\eta_{X\times Y},

  2. (SM2)

    stX,Y∘(idX×μY)=μX×Y∘T⁡(stX,Y)∘stX,T​Y\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{X}\times\mu_{Y})=\mu_{X\times Y}\circ T(\operatorname{st}_{X,Y})\circ\operatorname{st}_{X,TY},

  3. (SM3)

    and the associativity condition with the product associator, which in 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} is automatic.

The monad 𝒫+\mathscr{P}_{+} is strong for the Cartesian monoidal structure on 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}. Indeed, for any sets X,YX,Y, define

stX,Y:X×𝒫+​(Y)→𝒫+​(X×Y),(x,A)↦{(x,a):a∈A}(⊆X×Y).\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}:X\times\mathcal{P}_{+}(Y)\to\mathcal{P}_{+}(X\times Y),\quad(x,A)\mapsto\{(x,a):a\in A\}~(\subseteq X\times Y).

We have the following two facts:

  • •

    For (SM1), take any (x,y)∈X×Y(x,y)\in X\times Y. Then

    stX,Y⁡(x,ηY​(y))=stX,Y⁡(x,{y})={(x,y)}=ηX×Y​(x,y)\displaystyle\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}(x,\eta_{Y}(y))=\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}(x,\{y\})=\{(x,y)\}=\eta_{X\times Y}(x,y) (2.4)
  • •

    For (SM2), take any x∈Xx\in X and 𝒜∈𝒫+​(𝒫+​(Y))\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathcal{P}_{+}(Y)). Then we have

    stX,Y⁡(x,μY​(𝒜))=stX,Y⁡(x,⋃A∈𝒜A)={(x,y):y∈⋃A∈𝒜A}.\displaystyle\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}(x,\mu_{Y}(\mathcal{A}))=\operatorname{st}_{X,Y}\bigg(x,\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal{A}}A\bigg)=\bigg\{(x,y):y\in\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal{A}}A\bigg\}.

  • •

    The condition (SM3) follows similarly and is immediate from the associativity of the Cartesian product of sets.

For the purposes of this paper, we do not need the axioms (SM1)–(SM3).

Remark 2.5.

The powerset monad 𝒫+\mathscr{P}_{+} is commutative, i.e., for any A∈𝒫+​(X)A\in\mathcal{P}_{+}(X) and B∈𝒫+​(Y)B\in\mathcal{P}_{+}(Y), the two possible orders of applying the strength followed by μ\mu both yield the same subset A×B∈𝒫+​(X×Y)A\times B\in\mathcal{P}_{+}(X\times Y). Thus commutativity here is merely the fact that the Cartesian product of two non-empty subsets is independent of the order in which they are considered.

2.2 Convolutions of Kleisli morphisms

Definition 2.6.

Recall that a monoidal category consists of a category 𝐂\mathbf{C}, a bifunctor ⊗:𝐂×𝐂→𝐂\otimes:\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{C} called the tensor product, an object II called the unit, and three natural isomorphisms

αX,Y,Z:(X⊗Y)⊗Z→∼X⊗(Y⊗Z),λX:I⊗X→∼X,ρX:X⊗I→∼X,\alpha_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\xrightarrow{\sim}X\otimes(Y\otimes Z),\quad\lambda_{X}:I\otimes X\xrightarrow{\sim}X,\quad\rho_{X}:X\otimes I\xrightarrow{\sim}X,

called the associator, left unitor, and right unitor respectively. These are required to satisfy the pentagon and triangle identities, which ensure that the tensor product is associative and unital in a coherent manner.

Example 2.7.

The category 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} carries the Cartesian monoidal structure, where ⊗=×\otimes=\times is the usual Cartesian product, II is a one-point set, and the isomorphisms are the evident identifications

((x,y),z)↦(x,(y,z)),(∗,x)↦x,(x,∗)↦x.((x,y),z)\mapsto(x,(y,z)),\quad(*,x)\mapsto x,\quad(x,*)\mapsto x.

In this case the coherence axioms (SM1), (SM2) and (SM3) are automatically satisfied.

Example 2.9.

In the Cartesian monoidal category 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}, a monoid object is precisely a monoid in the usual algebraic sense. Indeed, a monoid object (H,m,e)(H,m,e) consists of a set HH, a map m:H×H→Hm:H\times H\to H which is associative, and a map e:{∗}→He:\{*\}\to H ({∗}\{*\} is a one-point set) which selects the identity element e⁡(∗)=1He(*)=1_{H} of HH. Thus, clearly, every group GG, with its group multiplication m:G×G→Gm:G\times G\to G and unit element 1G1_{G}, is also a monoid object in 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}.

Remark 2.17.

If the empty set is added, the complete lattice 𝒫⁡(G)\mathcal{P}(G) becomes a unital quantale: convolution distributes over arbitrary unions. The non-empty part used here is closed under convolution but is not a complete lattice. The distinction matters for representation questions, because the papers considered here use non-empty subsets.

3 Kleisli convolution representations

In this section, we introduce Kleisli convolution representations of semigroups into power semigroups of groups, generalising the classical notion of representations by subsets. We then establish a “base-change” theorem (see Theorem 3.7), showing that every surjective group homomorphism lifts a homomorphism of Kleisli convolution representations

3.1 Kleisli convolution representations of semigroups

Definition 3.1.

Let SS be a semigroup and GG a group. A Kleisli convolution representation of SS in GG is a homomorphism

ρ:S→Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+,fin)​(1,G),ρ⁡(s​t)=ρ⁡(s)⋆ρ⁡(t)\rho:S\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+,\mathrm{fin}})}(1,G),\quad\rho(st)=\rho(s)\star\rho(t)

of semigroups. It is faithful if it is injective and disjoint if ρ⁡(s)∩ρ⁡(t)=∅\rho(s)\cap\rho(t)=\varnothing whenever s≠ts\neq t.

Remark 3.2.

By Theorem 2.16, this is precisely a representation of SS in the convolution semigroup of the Kleisli points of the group object GG. Thus, an embedding S↪Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+,fin)​(1,G)S\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+,\mathrm{fin}})}(1,G) and a faithful Kleisli convolution representation are the same datum, not merely analogous data. In particular, when we think that 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) is a monoid, then the isomorphism θ+,G\theta_{+,G} provide a representation θ+,G−1:𝒫+​(G)​−−⟶≅⁡Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\theta_{+,G}^{-1}:\mathcal{P}_{+}(G)\mathop{-\!\!\!-\!\!\!\longrightarrow}\limits^{\cong}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) of 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G), obviously.

Remark 3.3.

For ρ⁡(s)⊆G\rho(s)\subseteq G, define a relation RR on S×GS\times G as follows:

s​R​g​ if and only if ​g∈ρ⁡(s).\displaystyle s~R~g\text{~if and only if~}g\in\rho(s). (3.1)

This gives a purely relational description of disjoint power-semigroup embeddings. The Kleisli convolution representation ρ:S→Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+,fin)​(1,G)\rho:S\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+,\mathrm{fin}})}(1,G) of a semigroup SS can be encoded equivalently as the relation (3.1). In this relational language, the homomorphism condition and the disjointness condition become, respectively:

  1. (A)

    Multiplication law: can be written without reference to ρ\rho as (s​t)​R​g(st)~R~g if and only if ∃x,y∈G\exists x,y\in G such that s​R​x,t​R​y, and ​g=x​y.sRx,\ tRy,\text{~and~}g=xy.

  2. (B)

    Disjointness: the converse relation Rop⊆G×SR^{\mathrm{op}}\subseteq G\times S is single-valued wherever it is defined.

See Table 1.

Conversely, given a relation RR on S×GS\times G satisfying (A) and (B) such that for every s∈Ss\in S, there is a g∈Gg\in G with s​R​gsRg. One recovers the representation by ρ⁡(s)={g∈G:s​R​g}\rho(s)=\{g\in G:s\,R\,g\}. Thus, a disjoint Kleisli convolution representation is the same datum as a relation whose multiplication law holds and whose converse is single-valued. The following is a theorem proved by Bershadsky and Kublanovsky [3, Theorem 1.1], expressed in the terminology above:

  • •

    ([3, Theorem 1.1, (1)]) every semigroup has a disjoint faithful Kleisli convolution representation in a symmetric group of sufficiently large degree;

  • •

    ([3, Theorem 1.1, (2)]) every semigroup also has a disjoint faithful Kleisli convolution representation in a free group with sufficiently many free generators.

3.2 Embeddings of Hom-spaces in Kleisli category

Let FF and GG be two groups and q:F→Gq:F\to G be a homomorphism of groups. For A⊆GA\subseteq G, write

q−1​(A):={x∈F:q⁡(x)∈A}.q^{-1}(A):=\{x\in F:q(x)\in A\}.
Lemma 3.4 ([3]).

For each group GG, we have 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) is a monoid.

Proof.

By Theorem 2.16, we have a bijection Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)→𝒫+​(G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G)\to\mathcal{P}_{+}(G), and 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) is a semigroup whose elements can be seen as Kleisli points in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G) and whose multiplication is induced by the convolution in Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,G)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,G). Moreover, 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) has an identity. Thus, 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) is a monoid. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

If a homomorphism q:F→Gq:F\to G of groups is surjective, then the following statements hold.

  1. (1)

    The map q−1:𝒫+​(G)→𝒫+​(F)q^{-1}:\mathcal{P}_{+}(G)\to\mathcal{P}_{+}(F) is an injective homomorphism of semigroups, i.e., q−1​(A⋆B)=q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)q^{-1}(A\star B)=q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B) for all non-empty subsets A,B⊆GA,B\subseteq G;

  2. (2)

    Disjoint families remain disjoint after applying q−1q^{-1}.

Proof.

First of all, we have that 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) and 𝒫+​(F)\mathcal{P}_{+}(F) are monoids by Lemma 3.4. By the definition of q−1q^{-1}, we have that q−1q^{-1} sends each A∈𝒫+​(G)A\in\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) to the subset q−1​(A)={x∈F:q⁡(x)∈A}q^{-1}(A)=\{x\in F:q(x)\in A\} of FF, then Im⁡(q−1)⊆𝒫+​(F)\operatorname{Im}(q^{-1})\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{+}(F), i.e., q−1q^{-1}, as a map from the monoid 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G) to the monoid 𝒫+​(F)\mathcal{P}_{+}(F), is well-defined.

Take two arbitrary subset AA and BB in 𝒫+​(G)\mathcal{P}_{+}(G). For any x∈q−1​(A)x\in q^{-1}(A) and y∈q−1​(B)y\in q^{-1}(B), we have q⁡(x​y)=q⁡(x)​q​(y)∈A⋆Bq(xy)=q(x)q(y)\in A\star B. It follows q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)⊆q−1​(A⋆B)q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B)\subseteq q^{-1}(A\star B). Conversely, take z∈q−1​(A⋆B)z\in q^{-1}(A\star B), we can find two element a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B such that q⁡(z)=a​bq(z)=ab. Since qq is surjective, there exists x∈Fx\in F with q⁡(x)=aq(x)=a, then q​(x)−1​q​(z)=q⁡(x−1​z)=a−1​a​b=bq(x)^{-1}q(z)=q(x^{-1}z)=a^{-1}ab=b, and so, x−1​z∈q−1​(B)x^{-1}z\in q^{-1}(B). Note that x∈q−1​(A)x\in q^{-1}(A), then z=x⋅x−1​z∈q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)z=x\cdot x^{-1}z\in q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B). It follows q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)⊇q−1​(A⋆B)q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B)\supseteq q^{-1}(A\star B). Therefore, we have q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)=q−1​(A⋆B)q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B)=q^{-1}(A\star B).

If q−1​(A)=q−1​(B)q^{-1}(A)=q^{-1}(B) and a∈Aa\in A, choose x∈Fx\in F with q⁡(x)=aq(x)=a. Then x∈q−1​(B)x\in q^{-1}(B), so a=q⁡(x)∈Ba=q(x)\in B. This proves A⊆BA\subseteq B, and the opposite inclusion is symmetric. Hence q−1q^{-1} is injective. Finally, inverse images preserve intersections, so they preserve disjointness. ∎

Now we illustrate Proposition 3.5 with a concrete example (using additive notation, since the groups involved are additive). This example shows that q−1q^{-1} may be not a homomorphism of monoids.

Example 3.6.

Let F=ℤF=\mathbb{Z}, G=ℤ/2​ℤ={0,1}G=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1\}, and q:ℤ→ℤ/2​ℤq:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} be the canonical quotient map n↦nmod2n\mapsto n\bmod 2. Then qq is surjective, and the inverse-image map q−1:𝒫+​(ℤ/2​ℤ)⟶𝒫+​(ℤ)q^{-1}:\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathbb{Z}) is given by

q−1​({0})={n∈ℤ:n​ is even}=2​ℤ,\displaystyle q^{-1}(\{0\})=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:n\text{ is even}\}=2\mathbb{Z},
q−1​({1})={n∈ℤ:n​ is odd}=2​ℤ+1,\displaystyle q^{-1}(\{1\})=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:n\text{ is odd}\}=2\mathbb{Z}+1,
q−1​({0,1})=ℤ.\displaystyle q^{-1}(\{0,1\})=\mathbb{Z}.

Thus q−1q^{-1} is an injective homomorphism of semigroups, as guaranteed by Proposition 3.5. For instance, we have q−1​({0})⋆q−1​({0})=2​ℤ+2​ℤ=2​ℤ=q−1​({0}⋆{0})q^{-1}(\{0\})\star q^{-1}(\{0\})=2\mathbb{Z}+2\mathbb{Z}=2\mathbb{Z}=q^{-1}(\{0\}\star\{0\}) because {0}⋆{0}={0}\{0\}\star\{0\}=\{0\} in 𝒫+​(ℤ/2​ℤ)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}). Similarly, for {0}\{0\} and {1}\{1\}, we have q−1​({0})⋆q−1​({1})=2​ℤ+(2​ℤ+1)=2​ℤ+1=q−1​({0}⋆{1})q^{-1}(\{0\})\star q^{-1}(\{1\})=2\mathbb{Z}+(2\mathbb{Z}+1)=2\mathbb{Z}+1=q^{-1}(\{0\}\star\{1\}), where {0}⋆{1}={1}\{0\}\star\{1\}=\{1\}. In this example, q−1q^{-1} does not preserve the monoid identity. The identity of 𝒫+​(ℤ/2​ℤ)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) is {0}\{0\}, while the identity of 𝒫+​(ℤ)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\mathbb{Z}) is {0}\{0\}. But q−1​({0})=2​ℤ≠{0}q^{-1}(\{0\})=2\mathbb{Z}\neq\{0\}. Therefore, q−1q^{-1} is a homomorphism of semigroups but not of monoids.

4 Kleisli category over finite powerset monad

In this section, we construct the reduced finite powerset monad on the category 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} of pointed sets, and prove that the reduced finitary power monoid 𝒫fin,1​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H) of a monoid HH is isomorphic to the Kleisli Hom-monoid Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H). This provide a Kleisli convolution representation of 𝒫fin,1​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H), and identification allows automorphism problems for reduced power monoids to be studied in the language of Kleisli categories.

4.1 Finite powerset monad and their Kleisli categories

Let H=(H,⋅)H=(H,\cdot) be a monoid. Recall that the reduced finitary power monoid of HH is

𝒫fin,1​(H):={A⊆H:A​ is finite and ​1∈A}.\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H):=\{A\subseteq H:A\text{ is finite and }1\in A\}.

To express this construction without changing the notation for its elements, we work in the category 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} of pointed sets.

For each set XX, we can define a pointed set (X,∗)(X,*) for an element ∗∈X*\in X. Here, we call ∗* is the basepoint. Now, we consider the pointed set category 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} whose objects are pointed sets and whose morphisms f:(X,∗)→(Y,∘)f:(X,*)\to(Y,\circ) are a map f:X→Yf:X\to Y with the basepoint condition f(∗)=∘f(*)=\circ. Note that there is a natural correspondence (X,∗)↦X(X,*)\mapsto X, which induces a faithful embedding 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭↪𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Set}. Clearly, it is a forgetful functor. In view of this embedding, 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} may be regarded as a subcategory of 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set}. For simplicity, we shall always treat 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} as a subcategory of 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} in our paper.

For a pointed set (X,∗)(X,*), we define

𝒫fin,∗(X,∗):=({A⊆X:A is finite and ∗∈A},{∗}).\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*):=\bigl(\{A\subseteq X:A\text{ is finite and }*\in A\},\{*\}\bigr).

and

  1. (𝒫fin\mathscr{P}_{\text{fin}}1)

    for any set pointed (X,∗)(X,*) in 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} and any x∈Xx\in X, η(X,∗)​(x):=ηX​(x)∪{∗}={x,∗}\eta_{(X,*)}(x):=\eta_{X}(x)\cup\{*\}=\{x,*\};

  2. (𝒫fin\mathscr{P}_{\text{fin}}2)

commutes.

In this paper, 𝒫fin,−\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-} denotes the reduced finite powerset functor on 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}, sending a pointed set (X,∗)(X,*) to 𝒫fin,∗(X,∗)={A⊆X:A finite and ∗∈A}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*)=\{A\subseteq X:A\text{ finite and }*\in A\}. Here the subscript “−-” is a placeholder for the basepoint. When evaluated at a concrete object (X,∗)(X,*), it is replaced by ∗*, yielding 𝒫fin,∗​(X,∗)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*). Similarly, 𝒫fin,−​(f)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-}(f) denotes the action of the functor on a morphism ff. Thus 𝒫fin,−\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-} is the abstract functor, while 𝒫fin,∗​(X,∗)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*) is its value at a specific object.

We have the following result which shows that the triple 𝒫fin=(𝒫fin,−,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}=(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-},\eta,\mu) is a monad.

Theorem 4.1.

The triple 𝒫fin=(𝒫fin,−,η,μ)\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}=(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-},\eta,\mu) is a monad over 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}.

We have show that 𝒫fin,−\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-} is a endofunctor on 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}, with action on morphisms given by direct image 𝒫fin,∗​(f)​(A)=f⁡[A]={f⁡(a):a∈A}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(f)(A)=f[A]=\{f(a):a\in A\} for any f:(X,∗)→(Y,∘)f:(X,*)\to(Y,\circ) and A∈𝒫fin,∗​(X,∗)A\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(X,*). This is well-defined because finite subsets are mapped to finite subsets, and f(∗)=∘f(*)=\circ ensures ∘∈f⁡[A]\circ\in f[A].

Next, for any morphism f:(X,∗)→(Y,∘)f:(X,*)\to(Y,\circ) in 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} and any x∈Xx\in X, we have

𝒫fin,−​(f)​(η(X,∗)​(x))=𝒫fin,−​(f)​({x,∗})={f⁡(x),f⁡(∗)}={f⁡(x),∘}=η(Y,∘)​(f⁡(x)).\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-}(f)(\eta_{(X,*)}(x))=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},-}(f)(\{x,*\})=\{f(x),f(*)\}=\{f(x),\circ\}=\eta_{(Y,\circ)}(f(x)).

4.2 Realising reduced finitary power monoids as Kleisli Hom-spaces

The following lemma shows that it is a monoid under the Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}) established in Theorem 4.1.

Lemma 4.2.

Under the Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}) of the monad 𝒫fin\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}, for every monoid HH as a set in 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}, pointed by its identity element 1H1_{H}, the set 𝒫fin,1H​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H) is a monoid (under the multiplication A⋆BA\star B, where the identity element is {1H}\{1_{H}\}).

Proof.

Let A,B∈𝒫fin,1H​(H)A,B\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H). Since AA and BB are finite, the set A⋆BA\star B is finite. Moreover, 1H=1H​1H∈A⋆B1_{H}=1_{H}1_{H}\in A\star B, and hence A⋆B∈𝒫fin,1H​(H)A\star B\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H).

On the other hand, for A,B,C∈𝒫fin,1H​(H)A,B,C\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H), the associativity of the multiplication of HH gives (A⋆B)⋆C={(ab)c:a∈A,b∈B,c∈C}={a(bc):a∈A,b∈B,c∈C}=A⋆(B⋆C)(A\star B)\star C=\{(ab)c:a\in A,\ b\in B,\ c\in C\}=\{a(bc):a\in A,\ b\in B,\ c\in C\}=A\star(B\star C). Finally, {1H}⋆A=A=A⋆{1H}\{1_{H}\}\star A=A=A\star\{1_{H}\}. Therefore, 𝒫fin,1H​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H) is a monoid with identity {1H}\{1_{H}\}. ∎

Let ℤ/2​ℤ=({0,1},0)\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=(\{0,1\},0) be a monoid given by addition “++”. In this case, the identity of it is 00. Of course, the group structure is mentioned here only to single out the natural basepoint 00; in the actual proof, we never use the fact that ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} is a group, and merely regard it as a two-element set {0,1}\{0,1\} with basepoint 00.

Lemma 4.3.

For every monoid HH in 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}, pointed by its identity element 1H1_{H}, the Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin,∗)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) is a monoid (under the operation (u⋆v)​(i):=u⁡(i)⋆v⁡(i)(u\star v)(i):=u(i)\star v(i) for i∈ℤ/2​ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}).

Proof.

By Theorem 4.1, we have established the Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}) on the monad Pfin,∗P_{\mathrm{fin},*}. This means that our discussion for Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) is valid. For u,v∈Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤCLOSEu,v\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, OPENH)H) and i∈ℤ/2​ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, define (u⋆v)​(i):=u⁡(i)⋆v⁡(i)(u\star v)(i):=u(i)\star v(i). By Lemma 4.2, u⁡(i)⋆v⁡(i)u(i)\star v(i) belongs to 𝒫fin,1H​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H). Moreover, since uu and vv are pointed maps, we have u⁡(0)=v⁡(0)={1H}u(0)=v(0)=\{1_{H}\}, and hence (u⋆v)​(0)={1H}⋆{1H}={1H}(u\star v)(0)=\{1_{H}\}\star\{1_{H}\}=\{1_{H}\}. Thus, u⋆vu\star v is a pointed map. For any u,v,wu,v,w and i∈ℤ/2​ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, we have ((u⋆v)⋆w)​(i)=(u⁡(i)⋆v⁡(i))⋆w⁡(i)=u⁡(i)⋆(v⁡(i)⋆w⁡(i))=(u⋆(v⋆w))​(i)((u\star v)\star w)(i)=(u(i)\star v(i))\star w(i)=u(i)\star(v(i)\star w(i))=(u\star(v\star w))(i). Therefore, the convolution is associative. The identity element is the pointed map 𝐞\mathbf{e} defined by 𝐞⁡(0)=𝐞⁡(1)={1H}\mathbf{e}(0)=\mathbf{e}(1)=\{1_{H}\}, since for any A∈𝒫fin,1H​(H)A\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H), {1H}⋆A=A=A⋆{1H}\{1_{H}\}\star A=A=A\star\{1_{H}\}. Thus, Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) is a monoid under convolution. ∎

Theorem 4.4.

For every monoid HH, pointed by its identity element 1H1_{H}, there is a natural bijection

θfin,H:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin,∗)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)→𝒫fin,1H​(H)\theta_{\mathrm{fin},H}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H)\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H)

of monoids. Under this identification, convolution is the usual product of reduced finite subsets.

Proof.

First of all, we have established the Kleisli category 𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}) in Theorem 4.1. Thus, we can use Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3 in this proof. By Lemma 4.2, we have that 𝒫fin,1H​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H) is a monoid, and by Lemma 4.3, we have that Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin,∗)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) is a monoid.

We restrict Theorem 2.16 from 𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{Set} to 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet} by requiring all subsets to contain the basepoint, and then further restrict to finite subsets. This yields a bijection θ\theta from Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin,∗)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},H) to 𝒫fin,1H​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1_{H}}(H). To be more precise, by Definition 2.1, a Kleisli morphism u:ℤ/2​ℤ↝Hu:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\rightsquigarrow H is a pointed map u:ℤ/2​ℤ→𝒫fin,∗​(H,1H)u:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(H,1_{H}) in 𝐏𝐒𝐞𝐭\mathbf{PSet}. Since ℤ/2​ℤ={0,1}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1\} has basepoint 00, the pointed condition gives u⁡(0)={1H}u(0)=\{1_{H}\}. Thus uu is determined solely by u⁡(1)u(1), which can be any element of 𝒫fin,∗​(H,1H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},*}(H,1_{H}). Hence evaluation at 11 gives the above bijection sending uu to a subset u⁡(1)u(1) of HH. Furthermore, by Theorem 2.16, this bijection identifies the convolution of Kleisli points with the usual subset product, i.e., A⋆B={ab:a∈A,b∈B}A\star B=\{ab:a\in A,\ b\in B\}. Then θfin,H\theta_{\mathrm{fin},H} is an isomorphism of monoids ∎

Remark 4.5.

In the additive case, the distinguished point is written 00 and 𝒫fin,1​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},1}(H) is correspondingly written 𝒫fin,0​(H)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(H). This is only the conventional additive replacement of the identity symbol, and no new object is introduced.

5 Faithful convolution representations

This section introduces faithful Kleisli convolution representations and a rigidity-transfer theorem for reduced finitary power monoids.

5.1 Faithful group models and rigidity transfer

Definition 5.1.

  1. (1)

    Let MM be a semigroup. We say that MM is rigid if every automorphism of MM is the identity automorphism, or equivalently, Aut⁡(M)={idM}\operatorname{Aut}(M)=\{\operatorname{id}_{M}\}.

  2. (2)

    More generally, a Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒯)​(B,H)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{T})}(B,H) is called rigid if it is rigid as a semigroup under convolution. If the convolution has an identity, then it is equivalently rigid as a monoid.

Remark 5.2.

Rigidity is invariant under semigroup isomorphisms. Indeed, if ρ:M→N\rho:M\to N is an isomorphism, then conjugation by ρ\rho gives a group isomorphism

Aut⁡(M)→Aut⁡(N),φ↦ρ​  ​φ​  ​ρ−1.\operatorname{Aut}(M)\to\operatorname{Aut}(N),\quad\varphi\mapsto\rho\ \lower-0.86108pt\hbox{\hbox to2.4pt{\vbox to2.4pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.2pt\lower-1.2pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 1.38 0 C 1.38 0.76 0.76 1.38 0 1.38 C -0.76 1.38 -1.38 0.76 -1.38 0 C -1.38 -0.76 -0.76 -1.38 0 -1.38 C 0.76 -1.38 1.38 -0.76 1.38 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\ \varphi\ \lower-0.86108pt\hbox{\hbox to2.4pt{\vbox to2.4pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.2pt\lower-1.2pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 1.38 0 C 1.38 0.76 0.76 1.38 0 1.38 C -0.76 1.38 -1.38 0.76 -1.38 0 C -1.38 -0.76 -0.76 -1.38 0 -1.38 C 0.76 -1.38 1.38 -0.76 1.38 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\ \rho^{-1}.

Consequently, MM is rigid if and only if NN is rigid.

Let SS be a numerical monoid, that is, an additive submonoid of ℕ={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\} with |ℕ0\S|<∞|\mathbb{N}_{0}\backslash S|<\infty. For simplicity, we define MS:=𝒫fin,0​(S)M_{S}:=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S). Its multiplication is the sumset convolution A⋆B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}A\star B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}. By Theorem 4.4, we have an isomorphism θfin,S:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)≅MS\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)\cong M_{S} of monoids.

The inclusion S⊆ℤS\subseteq\mathbb{Z} gives an injective homomorphism

MS↪⊆𝒫fin,0(ℤ),A↦AM_{S}\mathop{\hookrightarrow}\limits^{\subseteq}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(\mathbb{Z}),\quad A\mapsto A

of monoids. Thus, the reduced power monoid already has a canonical faithful convolution representation in a group.

Theorem 5.3.

  3. (3)

    For all A,B,X∈MSA,B,X\in M_{S}, A⋆X=B⋆XA\star X=B\star X if and only if ρq​(A)⋆ρq​(X)=ρq​(B)⋆ρq​(X)\rho_{q}(A)\star\rho_{q}(X)=\rho_{q}(B)\star\rho_{q}(X).

Proof.

Proposition 3.5, applied to qq, gives q−1​(A⋆B)=q−1​(A)⋆q−1​(B)q^{-1}(A\star B)=q^{-1}(A)\star q^{-1}(B). It also gives injectivity of ρq\rho_{q}, i.e., if q−1​(A)=q−1​(B)q^{-1}(A)=q^{-1}(B), then applying qq and using surjectivity yields A=BA=B. Thus, (1) holds. Hence ρq\rho_{q} is an isomorphism from MSM_{S} onto its image Im⁡(ρq)=ρq​(MS)\operatorname{Im}(\rho_{q})=\rho_{q}(M_{S}), and conjugation by any isomorphism induces the isomorphism of automorphism groups by Remark 5.2. Then we obtain (2). Finally, for all A,B,X∈MSA,B,X\in M_{S}, ρq​(A)⋆ρq​(X)=ρq​(B)⋆ρq​(X)\rho_{q}(A)\star\rho_{q}(X)=\rho_{q}(B)\star\rho_{q}(X) is preserved because ρq\rho_{q} is a homomorphism and reflected because it is injective. ∎

Remark 5.4.

Notice that ρq​({0})=Ker⁡(q)\rho_{q}(\{0\})=\operatorname{Ker}(q), which need not be the identity of 𝒫+​(F)\mathcal{P}_{+}(F) but is the identity inside the image ρq​(MS)\rho_{q}(M_{S}). This is why Theorem 5.3 (1) is naturally stated for semigroups, whereas the image Im⁡(ρq)=ρq​(MS)\operatorname{Im}(\rho_{q})=\rho_{q}(M_{S}) is nevertheless a monoid in its own right.

The isomorphism Aut⁡(MS)≅Aut⁡(ρq​(MS))\operatorname{Aut}(M_{S})\cong\operatorname{Aut}(\rho_{q}(M_{S})) given by Theorem 5.3 (2) implies that the rigidity of MSM_{S} can be reduced to the rigidity of ρq​(MS)\rho_{q}(M_{S}). The latter is isomorphic to a submonoid of 𝒫+​(F)\mathcal{P}_{+}(F), which, by Theorem 2.16, is equivalent to study some submonoid of Kleisli Hom-space Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫+)​(1,F)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{+})}(1,F). Furthermore, Theorem 5.3 shows that rigidity may be checked in any of the faithful group models above. What remains is to produce equations in the monoid that determine each finite subset. The next section does this without introducing an additional system of coordinates.

5.2 Application: Tringali–Yan Conjucture

Tringali and Yan conjectured in [24, Section 4] that the reduced finitary power monoid 𝒫fin,0​(S)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) is rigid for every numerical monoid SS properly contained in ℕ\mathbb{N}. This conjecture was proved by Bhowmik and Tringali in [4, Theorem 1.2]. Their proof is shorter than the proof given in this subsection. Some arguments below are Kleisli reformulations of the corresponding arguments in [4, Section 3]. More precisely, Lemma 5.5 is the Kleisli version of [4, Lemma 3.1], the second part of Lemma 5.6 is the Kleisli version of [4, Lemma 3.2], and Lemma 5.7 is the Kleisli version of [4, Lemma 3.4]. Our purpose here is not to claim another solution of the conjecture, but to present the relevant arguments in the language of Kleisli categories and to illustrate the possible applications of Kleisli convolution representations in semigroup theory.

Let SS be a numerical monoid and put MS=𝒫fin,0​(S)M_{S}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) as in Section 5. For every A∈MSA\in M_{S}, we define fA:=θfin,S−1​(A)f_{A}:=\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S}^{-1}(A) in this section, where

θfin,S:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)→≅MS\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S}\colon\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)\xrightarrow{\cong}M_{S}

is the isomorphism of monoids given in Theorem 4.4. Thus, fAf_{A} is the unique Kleisli arrow

fA:ℤ/2​ℤ↝Sf_{A}\colon\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\rightsquigarrow S

whose underlying map is given by

fA​(0)={0}andfA​(1)=A.f_{A}(0)=\{0\}\quad\text{and}\quad f_{A}(1)=A.

Let SS be a numerical monoid and put MS=𝒫fin,0​(S)M_{S}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) as in Section 5. For every A∈MSA\in M_{S}, we define fA:=θfin,S−1​(A)f_{A}:=\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S}^{-1}(A) in this section, where θfin,S\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S} is the isomorphism θfin,S:Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)→≅MS\theta_{\mathrm{fin},S}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)\xrightarrow{\cong}M_{S} of monoids given in Theorem 4.4. Obviously, fAf_{A} is the unique Kleisli arrow fA:ℤ/2​ℤ↝Sf_{A}:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\rightsquigarrow S whose underlying map fA:ℤ/2​ℤ→MS=𝒫fin,0​(S)f_{A}:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\to M_{S}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) is given by fA​(0)={0}f_{A}(0)=\{0\} and fA​(1)=Af_{A}(1)=A.

The following lemma is the Kleisli version of [4, Lemma 3.1].

Theorem 5.9.

Let SS be a numerical monoid properly contained in ℕ\mathbb{N}, then

Aut⁡(Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S))≅{1}.\operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S))\cong\{1\}.
Proof.

Take an arbitrary automorphism α∈Aut⁡(Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S))\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)) and an arbitrary Kleisli morphism f∈Hom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S), then there exists a unique A∈MSA\in M_{S} such that f=fAf=f_{A}. Since α⁡(fA)\alpha(f_{A}) is also an element of in same Kleisli Hom-space, there exists a unique A′∈MSA^{\prime}\in M_{S} such that α⁡(fA)=fA′\alpha(f_{A})=f_{A^{\prime}}. Then by Proposition 5.8, we have y∈Ay\in A if and only if y∈A′y\in A^{\prime} (y∈Sy\in S). Therefore, A=A′A=A^{\prime}, and hence α⁡(f)=α⁡(fA)=fA′=fA=f\alpha(f)=\alpha(f_{A})=f_{A^{\prime}}=f_{A}=f. By the arbitrariness of ff, we have α=idHom𝐊𝐥⁡(𝒫fin)​(ℤ/2​ℤ,S)\alpha=\operatorname{id}_{\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Kl}(\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{fin}})}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},S)} as required. ∎

Remark 5.10.

Tringali and Yan conjectured that 𝒫fin,0​(S)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin},0}(S) is rigid whenever SS is a numerical monoid properly contained in ℕ\mathbb{N} ([24, Section 4]). It is an easy consequence of Theorems 4.4 and 5.9 that the Tringali–Yan conjecture holds.
